newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Rescued UBS files detail property deals.
newsitem.headline: Rescued UBS files detail property deals.

text.p: Most of the documents rescued by former watchman Christoph Meili from shredding at Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) concern property maintenance and have nothing to do with dormant accounts of possible Holocaust victims, UBS said on Monday.

Meili, who turned over the UBS documents to Swiss Jews and then lost his job at a security firm, removed a total of 65 property files relating to 31 German properties owned by Eidgenoessische Bank between 1930 and 1945, UBS said on Monday.

The files throw light on the activities of Eidgenoessiche Bank, bought by UBS in 1945, in Germany prior to the outbreak of World War Two, including the acquisition of three properties, whose previous owners could have been Jewish.

"In the case of three properties, for the purchase of which a German bank in 1937 acted as intermediary and whose previous owners were possibly Jews, the minutes of the board of directors meetings and other documents are in existence," UBS said.

Whether the files are relevant in judging the business conduct of Eidgenoessiche Bank before and during the war is up to the Bergier Commission -- a panel of historians examining the Swiss role in World War Two, a UBS spokeswoman said.
UBS repeated that it regretted the destruction of documents, but added the comprehensive records still in existence provide excellent evidence of Eidgenoessiche Bank's properties.

The spokewoman also confirmed that all the files concerning the customers of Eidgenoessiche Bank -- and possible dormant accounts -- had been transferred to UBS' own files in 1945 and were never in danger of shredding.
Meili, who was hailed as a hero by U.S. Jewish leaders, had smuggled the bank documents out of UBS headquarters and passed them on to Jewish leaders, who alerted prosecutors in January.
Prosecutors are now investigating whether UBS broke a ban on destroying relevant records or if Meili violated Swiss banking secrecy.

Forty-nine of the 65 documents removed from UBS by Meili concern property maintenance, eight are account ledgers relating to mortgages, one is a list of 34 mortgages, three relate to property income in the 1950s and 1960s and four contain additional property information.
Forty-seven of the documents are from before and during World War Two, while 18 are from the 1950s through the 1970s.

Of the 31 properties that were owned by Eidgenoessiche Bank up to 1945, 20 were bought from a Swiss family, one was bought from a Swiss-controlled canning factory, one was bought from a private person in London, one was bought from a Berlin real estate company and five were acquired by auction from 1930 to 1934 and the previous owner was known in all cases.
